claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch through compositional adjustment enhances local lattice distortion in equimolar high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases hardness and strength relative to alloys having minimal atomic size differences.
The controlled comparison should use single-phase, homogeneous alloys with fine, controlled grain structures produced under identical processing conditions.
Composition should be varied systematically to change atomic size mismatch while holding processing, phase stability, and heat treatment constant.
Samples should be synthesized and heat treated identically and tested at room temperature under quasi-static loading.
Atomic size differences generate local lattice distortions.
Larger atomic size mismatches induce stronger local lattice strains.
Stronger local lattice strains hinder dislocation glide.
Hindered dislocation glide increases resistance to plastic deformation through solid-solution strengthening.
Alloys with higher average atomic size mismatch will have statistically significantly greater hardness than the minimal-mismatch baseline.
Alloys with higher average atomic size mismatch will have statistically significantly greater yield strength than the minimal-mismatch baseline.
An equimolar alloy with minimal atomic size differences will have lower lattice distortion.
Lower lattice distortion in the baseline will result in lower hardness and strength.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloys without competing effects from phase separation, precipitates, or very large grains.
The quantitative relationship between atomic size mismatch and mechanical-property enhancement may vary with elemental combination and processing variation.
Electron diffraction or high-resolution TEM can be used to quantify local lattice distortions in the comparison.
Failure of the higher-mismatch samples to show statistically significant increases in lattice distortion, hardness, and yield strength relative to the baseline is specified as a falsifying result.
